title: Data Encoding: Standard Encoding
summary: Standard encoding is the specific case of data encoding in which the adversary uses a published, widely implemented scheme that already fits the protocol in use. ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64 and MIME are the documented examples, and some schemes reduce size as well, as gzip compression does when combined with a text conversion. The important property is that the resulting blob is valid for the protocol, so a mail gateway or web proxy parsing the message sees nothing out of specification and no format rule is broken. The parent technique covers encoding in general, including custom and non standard approaches; this sub-technique is the case where a defender can decode the content with an ordinary tool once they suspect it is there. Detection therefore combines protocol aware inspection with statistical signals such as long strings drawn from a tiny alphabet, unusual padding characters, and payload sizes that do not match the application's normal use.

beginner.definition: Standard encoding means using a well known rule, such as Base64, to change data into another form. Anyone who has the same rule can change it back again. The parent technique covers encoding in general. This sub-technique is the case where the scheme is a common, published one.
beginner.whyItMatters: Standard schemes are built into many programs, so the attacker needs no special software. The result is valid for the protocol, so mail and web filters see an ordinary message. Because the rule is public, a defender can decode the content quickly once it is found. The hard part is noticing it, not reading it.
howItWorks: The attacker chooses a published scheme such as Base64, hexadecimal, ASCII, Unicode or MIME.
The command and control data is then converted into that encoded form by the tool.
The encoded text is placed in a field the protocol normally carries. Examples are a form field or a message header.
Because the scheme is standard, the message stays valid and passes format checks.
Some implementations also compress the payload before encoding it, or after decoding it.
The receiving tool reverses the public rule and runs the instruction it recovers.
beginner.example: Imagine an office where staff write notes in a standard shorthand that everyone in the trade learns. A note in shorthand on a desk looks completely normal, because shorthand is common in that office. Anyone who knows the system can read it in a moment. The difficulty is not reading the note, it is noticing that the note exists at all.
takeaways: Standard encoding produces valid protocol content, so format checks pass it.
Once it is found, standard encoding is easy to reverse with common tools.
Small alphabets and regular padding are useful clues in network data.

objectives: Explain what standard encoding means and how it differs from the parent technique.
Name five standard encoding schemes that can carry command and control data.
Describe why standard encoding survives protocol validation.
Explain how a defender can decode suspicious standard encoded content.
Identify network features that suggest an encoded payload.
